n: In this lesson we will learn to determine carboxyhaemoglobin, that is, COHb, in blood by the spectrophotometric method. The plan is as follows: carbon monoxide poisoning, methods of determining COHb, the theory of spectrophotometry, measurement on the UV-1900 instrument, calculation and control. Key terms: COHb, deoxyhaemoglobin, sodium dithionite, isosbestic point, Base Corr. and Photometric 8l. The aim of the lesson is the analysis of COHb in blood by a chemical and a physico-chemical, that is, spectrophotometric, method. The working order is as follows: preparation, calibration, sample, measurement, calculation and cleaning.

t: Sources of carbon monoxide and dangerous concentrations
n: Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas. Its mixture with air from 16 to 73 % can explode. It is formed when organic substances, coal, gas and other fuels burn incompletely. In natural gas, carbon monoxide is 4-30 %, and in "water gas" 40-50 %. In an explosion, about 30 % carbon monoxide is formed. In the air of homes and workplaces, 0.07-0.08 % carbon monoxide is dangerous to life. The permissible concentration is 0.02 mg/l. Remember the difference between these figures well.

t: Forms of haemoglobin in the blood
n: In the blood of a poisoned person, three kinds of compounds may be present: deoxyhaemoglobin, symbol Hb; oxyhaemoglobin, symbol OHb; and carboxyhaemoglobin, symbol COHb. Deoxyhaemoglobin is the form without oxygen and without carbon monoxide. Oxyhaemoglobin is bound to oxygen, and carboxyhaemoglobin is bound to carbon monoxide. Methaemoglobin, that is, MtHb, may also be partly present; it does not bind carbon monoxide. Remember: if carboxyhaemoglobin is found in the blood, it proves that the patient was poisoned with carbon monoxide.

t: Binding of carbon monoxide to haemoglobin
n: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin very easily and forms stable carboxyhaemoglobin. The reaction is written thus: HbO2 plus CO gives HbCO plus O2. That is, carbon monoxide takes the place of the oxygen in oxyhaemoglobin. The rate of binding is 300 times stronger than that of oxygen, and the release of CO is 3600 times slower. Because carbon monoxide has no smell, poisoning occurs quickly and suddenly. This is why it is so dangerous.

t: COHb content and degree of poisoning
n: The degree of poisoning depends on the COHb content in the blood. If COHb is 20-30 %, poisoning is mild. At 30-35 % poisoning is moderate, and at 35-50 % severe. At 50-60 % strong poisoning is observed: convulsions and loss of consciousness. When 70-80 % is reached, death occurs. This table is needed to interpret the result in forensic medical assessment.

t: Signs on the body and elimination of carbon monoxide
n: Now the signs on the body. Cadaveric lividity and blood are bright red because of carboxyhaemoglobin. The liver, kidneys and lungs are reddened, and signs of haemorrhage are found in the brain tissues. Carbon monoxide is eliminated from the body only through the respiratory tract. Opinions differ about how long it persists: according to one view it persists up to 122 days, according to another it can no longer be detected after 25-40 hours.

The detection of carbon monoxide is based on determining carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood by chemical and physico-chemical methods. Physico-chemical methods include spectroscopic, spectrophotometric, photometric and gas chromatographic methods. In the chemical method, the change of colour is compared. In the spectroscopic method, Fraunhofer lines are seen, while the spectrophotometric method works in the 450-620 nm region. To determine it from a biological object, the object is crushed, the blood is separated, and then the blood is examined.

In the spectroscopic method, the blood is examined in a spectroscope, and Fraunhofer lines are seen in the D and E region of the spectrum. COHb produces absorption in the regions 564-579 and 523-536 nm. Ammonium sulphide is used to establish the difference. Under its action, the absorption of OHb merges into one broad band in the range 543-596 nm, that is, oxyhaemoglobin is reduced. The spectrum of COHb, however, does not change; it is not reduced by ammonium sulphide.

The essence of the spectrophotometric method is that OHb and COHb are reduced to deoxyhaemoglobin and the absorbance is determined. Identity and quantity are determined from the absorption spectra in the wavelength region 450-620 nm. Three solutions are prepared: A, the blood under test; B, COHb plus deoxy; C, COHb only. For solution A, 1 ml of blood is diluted to 100 ml, buffer pH 7.38. Cuvette thickness 1 cm.

Determining the quantity of substances by their absorption of light is called photometry. Its types: colorimetry, photocolorimetry and spectrophotometry. In colorimetry, comparison is made visually or with a device. In photocolorimetry, polychromatic light, the visible part of the spectrum, is used. Spectrophotometry, however, is based on determination in monochromatic light in the visible region and the adjacent ultraviolet region. The dependence of light absorption on wavelength is called the absorption spectrum of the substance. Unlike photocolorimetry, spectrophotometry makes it possible to work over a wide wavelength range and with great accuracy.

In the book the equation of absorbance is written in the form D equals E multiplied by l multiplied by C. Here E is the molar absorption coefficient. At the wavelength of maximum absorption E is always the largest. The absorbance of the solution under test should lie in the range from 0.2 to 1.0. For COHb the cuvette is 1 cm. Pesticides at a concentration of 10-100 µg/ml obey the general Bouguer-Lambert-Beer law, at a layer thickness of 10 mm.

t: Why measurement is made at the wavelength of the maximum
n: Why is the measurement made at the wavelength of the maximum? The absorbance is measured at the wavelength corresponding to the maximum absorption of the solution under test. First the spectrum of the solution is taken, then lambda maximum is found. The absorbance is measured at this wavelength, because at the maximum E is greatest. As a result, the sensitivity and accuracy of measuring absorbance increase. Monochromatic light is isolated with the help of monochromators.

We will consider spectrophotometry using caffeine as an example. To prepare the standard solution, 0.1 g of caffeine is weighed on an analytical balance and dissolved in ethyl alcohol in a 100 ml volumetric flask. The absorption spectrum is measured at wavelengths 200-400 nm. Caffeine in ethyl alcohol has a maximum at 273 nm. The absorbance of caffeine isolated from the object is also measured at 273 nm, and the reference solution is ethyl alcohol. At the end, the spectra are recorded in the laboratory notebook.

Now we get acquainted with the instrument itself. The wavelength range of the UV-1900 series is 190-1100 nm; in the appendix the manual is given for the UV-1900i. The light source is a WI lamp, that is, halogen, or a D2 lamp, that is, deuterium. The state of the lamp is shown in the status panel at the top of the screen. The mass of the instrument is 16.6 kg. At the installation site, the temperature should be 15-35 °C and the humidity 35-80 %, and the place should be free from direct sunlight and vibration.

In the mode menu of the UV-1900i there are six modes: Photometric, Spectrum, Quantitation, Kinetics, Time Course and Bio Method. The Photometric mode measures absorbance and transmittance at one or several wavelengths. In the Photometric 8l mode, 2-8 wavelengths are used. The Spectrum mode takes a spectrum by scanning the wavelength; peak picking and smoothing are possible. Quantitation gives the quantity from a calibration line, while Kinetics and Time Course show the change over time.

The Quantitation mode builds a calibration curve from standard samples and quantitatively determines an unknown sample. There are four measurement methods: measurement at one, two and three wavelengths, and the derivative, that is, Derivative, method. There are three calibration methods: K Factor, 1 Point Curve and Multi-Point Curve. That is, first the measurement method is chosen, then the calibration method.

In multi-wavelength measurement, one of five equations is chosen on the basis of values at not more than four wavelengths. In the Photometric 8l mode, not more than eight wavelengths are set. The first equation is A1 minus A2, the second A1 divided by A2. The third is dA, that is, from A1 to A3. In the fourth and fifth equations the coefficients K1 to K5 take part: in the fourth the sum is multiplied by K5, in the fifth the ratio of two sums is taken.

Which mode is needed for COHb? Measurement is made at two wavelengths, D1 and D2, so the Photometric 8l mode is suitable, in which 2-8 wavelengths are entered. In this mode the wavelengths are measured in sequence and the result is seen in a table. In the Spectrum mode, however, the scanning range is entered, the spectrum is drawn in real time and peak picking, that is, Peak Pick, is possible. The teacher approves this setting.

Before start-up there must be no cuvettes in the instrument: otherwise the light will be blocked and an error may occur in the check. The cuvette compartment and the holder are empty. Then the power button is pressed. After switching on, checks and initialisation begin, after which the Mode Menu screen appears. If the security mode is on, the login screen appears after initialisation. The state of the WI or D2 lamp is seen in the status panel.

The power supply is 100-240 VAC, 140 VA, 50/60 Hz. The instrument must be earthed, and the cable supplied in the set should be used. At least 100 mm of free space is left from the left side of the instrument to the wall, because the fan is there. In an emergency the power button is moved to the "○" position and the mains cable is disconnected. The cover of the instrument must not be opened, its parts must not be replaced and it must not be repaired by oneself; a Shimadzu representative is contacted.

Distinguish the three solutions. A is the solution of the blood under test: 1 ml of blood is diluted to 100 ml with pH 7.38 buffer or 0.1 % ammonia. B is solution A with sodium dithionite added, using 3-4 mg of Na dithionite; in it OHb is completely reduced to deoxyhaemoglobin. C is the solution saturated with CO: OHb passes completely into COHb. Here 5-7 mg of Na dithionite is added, and to reduce MtHb it is saturated with CO again.

Solution A is prepared as follows. To 1 ml of blood without sediment, pH 7.38 phosphate buffer or 0.1 % ammonia solution is added up to 100 ml and mixed well. Attention is paid to the colour of the solution obtained being clear; the solution must be clear. Ammonia variant: the blood is placed in a 100 ml volumetric flask and made up to the mark with 0.1 % ammonia.

For solution C, CO is first generated: from concentrated sulphuric acid and formic acid, that is, H2SO4 plus HCOOH. The CO formed is first passed through 10 % alkali, which retains HCOOH vapour. Then it is passed through water, to free it of alkali. After that the gas is sent into the vessel with solution A. Then 5-7 mg of sodium dithionite is added, and it is saturated once more with additional CO.

The prepared solution is placed in a 1 cm spectrophotometer cuvette. As the reference, 0.1 % ammonia is used; it may also be the buffer with which the blood was diluted, or water. Crystals of sodium hydrosulphite are added to the cuvette, the cap is closed and it is shaken.

t: Setting zero: Auto Zero and Base Corr.
n: The cover of the cuvette compartment must be closed during measurement and zero setting. There are two kinds of zero setting. Auto Zero works only at a set wavelength. Baseline Correction, however, introduces a correction over a set wavelength interval. Before the first measurement, an empty, that is, blank, sample is placed in the cuvette and [Auto Zero] or [Base Corr.] is pressed. In the Photometric mode, 0 Abs, that is, 100 %T, is set. In the Spectrum and 8l modes, Base Corr. is used. After this, Start is pressed.

Measurement in Photometric, that is, single-wavelength, mode. After the parameters are set, before the first measurement a blank is placed in the cuvette and [Auto Zero] is pressed; the value becomes 0 Abs, that is, 100 % T. Then the unknown sample is placed and [Start] is pressed. At most 400 measurements can be made at one time. During measurement only [Stop] works. The result shows the photometric value and K multiplied by the photometric value; by changing K with [Recalc.], it can be recalculated.

Parameters of the Spectrum mode. Photometric Type: Abs, %T, %R or Energy. Scan Range: the starting wavelength must be greater than the end. Scan Speed has five options: Survey, Fast, Medium, Slow and Very Slow. Data Interval is AUTO or 0.05-2.0 nm. The number of points may be up to 2001; if it is exceeded, the interval is changed automatically.

The procedure for measuring the spectrum. First the parameters are set in [Scan Settings] and [Measurement Settings]. Then [Base Corr.] is performed with the blank, after which solutions B and C are placed in the cuvette and [Start] is pressed. During measurement the spectrum is drawn in real time; it can be stopped only with [Stop]. After measurement the graph is enlarged. Peak picking, smoothing and arithmetic operations may be applied.

t: Viewing, saving and processing the spectrum
n: During measurement the spectrum is drawn in real time; stopping only with [Stop]. The cursor, that is, the orange vertical line, shows the wavelength and photometric value at the selected point. The display range of the graph is changed by entering the upper and lower limits and pressing [Apply]. [Save Curve] saves the measured data, [Print] prints. In [Operations] there are Arithmetic, Derivative, Peak Pick and others. A saved curve is opened in [View] through [Load Curve].

Now the expected spectra. Deoxyhaemoglobin, that is, solution B, gives one maximum at 557 nm. COHb has two maxima at 541 and 571 nm. On the overall plot, the formation of isosbestic points at 550, 565 and 580 nm is characteristic. Remember: one maximum is characteristic of deoxyhaemoglobin, two maxima of carboxyhaemoglobin.

In quantitative measurement, absorbance is measured in two monochromatic beams, D1 and D2. At these two places the difference between COHb and Hb is greatest. D2 is measured at 550 nm, that is, at the isosbestic point. For D1, 538 nm was adopted; in some places in the book 534 nm is written. The coefficient K equals 0.372, the cuvette is 1 cm, and the dithionite in solution B is 3-4 mg.

t: Measuring two wavelengths on the UV-1900i
n: Measuring two wavelengths on the UV-1900i. First, from Photometric, the Photometric 8l mode is selected. [No. of WLs] is from 2 to 8; here it is 2. The wavelengths are 538 and 550 nm; the teacher approves this. Measurement is made in the order [WL1], [WL2]. Before the first measurement, [Base Corr.] is pressed with the blank, then [Start]. The results are seen in [Photo. Table]; they are saved with [Save Table] and printed with [Print].

The COHb content is calculated by the following formula: P equals 100 minus D_COHb minus D_HbCOHb, multiplied by 100, divided by D_HbI multiplied by K. Here K equals 0.372. P is the COHb content, in per cent. D_COHb is the absorbance at 538 nm of solution C, saturated with CO. D_HbCOHb is the absorbance of solution B after dithionite. D_HbI is the absorbance of solution B at 550 nm, that is, at the isosbestic point.

The result obtained serves for the forensic medical assessment of carbon monoxide poisoning. If COHb is found in the blood, it proves that the patient was poisoned with carbon monoxide. We assess the degree by the table in the book: 20-30 % is mild poisoning, and 70-80 % is death.

In chemical methods, the colours of poisoned and pure blood are compared: blood containing COHb does not change colour. With copper sulphate, that is, CuSO4 10 %, blood with COHb becomes bright red, pure blood green. With NaOH 30 %, blood with COHb is bright red, pure blood brown. With formaldehyde 40 %, pure blood becomes brownish-black in 5-10 minutes. With lead acetate 5 %, pure blood is brown. With K3[Fe(CN)6] 1 %, pure blood turns yellow.

t: Additional colour reactions: pure blood and COHb
n: The chemical methods are based on the greater stability of carboxyhaemoglobin compared with oxyhaemoglobin. Normal blood, when diluted with water, becomes brown, while blood with COHb does not change its bright red colour. In caustic alkali, pure blood becomes bluish black, and blood with COHb keeps its colour. With tannin, a grey substance forms in pure blood. With lead acetate, pure blood takes on a dirty blue colour, with formalin a dirty brown, while in blood with COHb there is no change.

Limitations of the methods. To confirm the presence of COHb in blood, several reactions are compared; a single reaction can lead to error. In mild poisoning the reagents give the same result as with unpoisoned blood, so chemical methods are of little value at low COHb. In putrefied blood a bright red colour, that is, haemochromogen, forms with NaOH even when there is no COHb. Spectrophotometry, however, gives identity and quantity, and the absorbance of the solution must be from 0.2 to 1.0.

Safety rules. Toxic or biologically hazardous samples are handled wearing protective gloves and goggles. If a sample is spilled, it is removed by the method in the SDS, and the room is ventilated. No reagent is placed on the instrument. Alcohol or solvent is not used when cleaning the instrument. Spilled water is not left.

t: Safety and quality control: COHb analysis
n: Quality control points. The solutions A, B and C obtained must be clear; clarity is checked after the reagent is added. The absorbance must be within 0.2-1.0. The cover of the cuvette compartment is closed during measurement and zero setting. Zero, that is, the blank, is set before the first measurement. Toxic and biologically hazardous samples are handled in gloves and goggles. Do not rely on a single reaction: to confirm the presence of COHb in blood, several reactions are compared.

A situational problem. 10 ml of blood is submitted: pink patches on the body, the blood in the internal organs very fluid, of a red-scarlet colour. The event: died by drowning in the bath at home. Determine which toxic substance caused the poisoning. The results of the chemical reactions are entered in a "wheel" table.

Five questions for review. First: explain the action of carbon monoxide on the human body and the ways of eliminating it from the body. Second: at what amount of carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood may the patient die? Third: which physico-chemical methods are known for the qualitative and quantitative determination of carbon monoxide in blood? Fourth: which colour reactions are recommended for determining carbon monoxide in blood? Fifth: on what, and on which processes, is the spectrophotometric determination of carbon monoxide in blood based?
